llmcost.q: What are the two kinds of tokens an LLM API call is billed for?
options: Input tokens you send and output tokens the model writes
Cached tokens and uncached tokens only
Words in the prompt and characters in the answer
Tokens per second and tokens per minute
llmcost.why: Every call charges for input tokens (instructions, history, documents) and output tokens, each at its own price per million.

llmcost.q: Why do teams report p95 latency instead of only the average?
options: p95 is always lower, so it looks better in reports
The average hides the slow tail that real users feel
Providers only bill by p95
p95 measures cost, not time
llmcost.why: p95 is the time 95% of requests beat, so it shows how bad the slow requests are. An average can look fine while many users wait.

llmcost.q: Brightfield Insurance's claims bot is too expensive. Most questions are simple lookups. What change usually cuts cost most safely?
options: Switch every call to the biggest model for accuracy
Remove the system prompt entirely
Route easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large one
Raise max_tokens so answers finish in one call
llmcost.why: Routing sends the easy majority to a cheaper, faster model while keeping the large model for hard cases, so cost drops without hurting quality.

llmcost.q: Every call at Kestrel Logistics starts with the same 6,000-token policy manual. What helps most with cost and speed?
options: Paraphrase the manual differently on each call
Move the manual after the user question
Split the manual across ten separate calls
Use prompt caching on that identical prefix
llmcost.why: Prompt caching stores the processed identical prefix, so repeat calls read it cheaply and faster. It only works if the prefix is exactly the same.

llmcost.q: A teammate puts the current timestamp and user name at the very start of every prompt. Why is this a mistake?
options: It makes the prefix differ each call, so cache hits never happen
Timestamps are not allowed by LLM providers
It makes the answer shorter than it should be
It forces the model to stream its output
llmcost.why: Caching matches an exact prefix. Changing text at the start breaks it every time, so put variable details after the stable block.

options: A library for training neural networks faster
Practices for getting models into production and keeping them healthy
A type of GPU used for inference
A dashboard showing server uptime
mlops.why: MLOps covers the whole model lifecycle: data, training, registry, deployment, monitoring and retraining.

options: A model file being copied to the wrong folder
A slow database query
A change in the inputs the model sees compared with training data
Labels arriving late from the customer
mlops.why: Data drift means live inputs no longer look like the training data, for example a new customer segment, which can quietly hurt accuracy.

mlops.q: Harlow Bank wants a new fraud model live next week, but fears it behaves badly on real traffic. What is a low-risk first step?
options: Replace the old model for all users at once
Skip testing because the test set score was good
Shadow deploy: log its predictions on real traffic while users get the old model
Retrain it daily until it looks stable
mlops.why: A shadow deploy shows how the new model behaves on live traffic with zero user impact. A canary can follow with a small share of users.

mlops.q: A churn model at Pinecrest Telecom was great in testing but is weak in production. Features were rewritten for the live service. Likely cause?
options: The GPU was too small for inference
Training-serving skew: features are computed differently in each place
The model registry lost its version number
Users stopped logging in
mlops.why: When training and serving compute features differently, the model sees unfamiliar inputs live. A shared feature definition or feature store prevents this.

mlops.q: Which setup is the classic MLOps trap?
options: Logging parameters and metrics for each experiment run
Storing approved models with versions in a registry
Monitoring input distributions as well as accuracy
Auto-retraining on a schedule and deploying with no eval gate
mlops.why: Without an evaluation gate, one bad data week can ship a worse model automatically. Always compare against the current model before deploying.

mlmetrics.q: In a fraud model, what does recall measure?
options: Share of flagged cases that were really fraud
Share of all real fraud cases the model caught
Share of all predictions that were correct
How fast the model scores a transaction
mlmetrics.why: Recall is caught fraud divided by all real fraud. Precision is the share of flags that were right.

mlmetrics.q: What does the classification threshold do?
options: Sets how much training data to use
Measures model speed
Turns the model's score into a yes or no decision
Chooses which features to keep
mlmetrics.why: Moving the threshold trades false alarms against misses, so it should reflect what each error costs.

mlmetrics.q: Ashford Bank's churn model shows 97% accuracy, but only 3% of customers churn. What do you check first?
options: Precision and recall on the churners, from the confusion matrix
Whether accuracy can reach 99%
The model's training time
How many features the model uses
mlmetrics.why: A model that predicts 'no churn' for everyone scores 97% here. Rare events need precision, recall and the confusion matrix.

mlmetrics.q: At a hospital, missing a sepsis case is far worse than a false alarm. How should you set the threshold?
options: Keep the default 0.5
Raise it to cut false alarms
Pick it at random and review later
Lower it to catch more cases, accepting more false alarms
mlmetrics.why: When misses are costly, favour recall. Choose the threshold from the real cost of each error type.

mlmetrics.q: A teammate tuned the threshold on the test set and then reported test scores. Why is that a problem?
options: Test sets must never be used at all
The scores look better than they will be in production
Thresholds cannot be tuned
It makes the model train slower
mlmetrics.why: Tuning on the test set leaks it into your choices. Tune on a validation set and keep the test set for the final, honest score.

options: Turning images of text, like scans, into machine-readable text
A way to compress PDFs
A database for storing documents
A method for translating documents
docai.why: OCR (optical character recognition) reads text from images. PDFs that already contain text do not need it.

docai.q: Why extract document fields into a fixed schema?
options: It makes the PDF smaller
It removes the need for any review
Downstream systems get consistent, checkable fields
It lets the model skip reading the text
docai.why: A schema gives every field a name and type, so you can validate values with rules and load them into other systems.

docai.q: Carden Insurance sends 50,000 PDFs; most are digital, some are scans. How do you process them cheaply?
options: Send every page to a vision model
Extract text directly where it exists and OCR only the scans
Retype them by hand
Convert all pages to images first
docai.why: Most digital PDFs already contain clean text. OCR or vision only where needed saves cost and errors.

docai.q: An extraction model returns invoice totals that look tidy but a few are wrong. What should the pipeline add?
options: A bigger model and nothing else
Faster OCR
More PDFs in the batch
Rule checks like line items summing to the total, with doubtful cases sent to a person
docai.why: Tidy output is not proof. Schema checks, business rules and a human review path catch errors before they spread.

docai.q: Which document pipeline choice is the trap?
options: Keeping table structure when parsing
Validating fields against a schema
Flattening tables to plain text and letting the model guess which number is which
Routing low-confidence fields to review
docai.why: Flattened tables lose which value belongs to which row and column. Keep the layout so numbers stay attached to labels.

serving.q: What is VRAM, and why does it matter for serving open models?
options: Disk space for logs; it limits history
GPU memory; the weights and working memory must fit in it
Network bandwidth; it limits users
CPU cache; it sets the tokenizer speed
serving.why: An open model's weights plus its working memory, like the KV cache, must fit in the GPU's memory.

serving.q: What does an inference server like vLLM mainly add?
options: Batches many requests together so the GPU is used efficiently
Trains the model on customer data
Replaces the need for a GPU
Writes prompts for users
serving.why: Batching concurrent requests keeps the GPU busy and raises throughput far above one request at a time.

serving.q: Stonebridge Health must keep patient data inside its own network. Which option fits?
options: A public hosted API with default settings
Emailing data to a vendor for batch processing
Self-host an open-weight model on their own GPUs
Skip AI for this use case entirely
serving.why: Self-hosting gives control over where data goes, at the cost of running the GPUs and servers yourself.

serving.q: A model fit on the GPU in testing but crashes with out-of-memory once users send long prompts. Likely cause?
options: The tokenizer is too slow
The model weights changed
The server has too few CPU cores
The GPU was sized for weights only, not the growing KV cache
serving.why: Long prompts and many users grow the working memory. Size for weights plus KV cache at real concurrency.

serving.q: A team compares self-hosting to an API using only the hourly GPU price. What are they missing?
options: Engineer time, idle capacity and upgrade work
The model's parameter count
The API's documentation quality
Nothing, GPU price is the full cost
serving.why: Self-hosting has hidden costs. A fair comparison includes people, idle GPUs and maintenance.

frameworks.q: At its core, what is an agent loop?
options: A scheduled batch job
Call the model, run the tools it asks for, feed results back, repeat
A database trigger
A chain of fixed prompts with no tools
frameworks.why: Frameworks package parts of this loop. Understanding the raw loop helps you judge whether you need one.

frameworks.q: When is adopting an agent framework worth it?
options: Whenever it is the most popular choice
Always, for any LLM feature
When it removes real work you would otherwise write and maintain
Never, frameworks are always harmful
frameworks.why: Pick a framework for real value like state, retries or tracing, not because it is trendy.

frameworks.q: Wexford Bank needs a three-step extraction flow and has a strict security review. What do you suggest?
options: A small direct loop using the model SDK, easy to review
The largest framework with every plugin enabled
Three different frameworks for flexibility
A custom framework built from scratch over months
frameworks.why: For a simple flow, a thin direct loop keeps prompts visible and the security review small.

frameworks.q: A customer's agent gives odd answers, and nobody can see the exact prompt the framework sends. First step?
options: Switch to a bigger model
Add more tools
Rewrite the whole app in another framework
Turn on tracing or logging to see the exact prompt and tool schemas
frameworks.why: You cannot debug what you cannot see. Inspect what the model actually receives before changing anything else.

frameworks.q: Which framework decision is the trap?
options: Checking who will maintain the code
Choosing by popularity instead of the customer's language, hosting and security needs
Reviewing the framework's tracing support
Starting with a simple loop and adding a library later
frameworks.why: The right choice depends on the customer's constraints and who owns the code after you leave.

graphrag.q: How does a knowledge graph store facts?
options: As entities joined by named relationships
As long text chunks with embeddings
As rows in a spreadsheet
As images of documents
graphrag.why: For example: Supplier A SUPPLIES Part B. This lets you follow connections across many facts.

options: Increasing image resolution before OCR
Deleting old entities from the graph
Merging different mentions of the same thing into one node
Ranking entities by popularity
graphrag.why: Without it, 'Acme Corp' and 'ACME Inc.' become separate nodes and connections are lost.

graphrag.q: Halden Pharma asks: 'Which of our suppliers depend on a factory affected by the flood?' Why might GraphRAG help?
options: The question is a single-fact lookup
It needs several connected facts across documents
Graphs are always faster than vector search
It avoids needing any documents
graphrag.why: Multi-hop questions need linked facts that plain chunk retrieval often misses.

graphrag.q: A team wants a knowledge graph for an HR bot where users ask 'How many vacation days do I get?'. Your advice?
options: Build the graph first, it is always better
Use both a graph and three vector stores
Replace documents with a graph entirely
Start with plain RAG; these are simple lookups it handles well
graphrag.why: Graphs add cost and complexity. Use them when questions truly need connected facts.

graphrag.q: Your LLM-built graph has 4,000 relationship types like 'supplies', 'supplier_of' and 'provides_to'. What went wrong?
options: The LLM could invent any label instead of using a fixed set
Too few documents were used
The graph database is too slow
Entity names were too short
graphrag.why: Give the LLM a fixed list of allowed relationship types so the graph stays consistent and queryable.

multimodal.q: What does a voice agent chain together?
options: Only a text-to-speech model
Image model, OCR and a database
Voice detection, speech-to-text, an LLM with tools, and text-to-speech
A phone line and a recorded menu
multimodal.why: Each stage adds delay, so the whole round trip must stay near one second to feel natural.

options: Turns spoken audio into written text
Reads text aloud
Translates between languages
Detects the speaker's mood only
multimodal.why: Speech-to-text (transcription) lets the LLM work with what the caller said.

multimodal.q: Callers at Tidewater Couriers complain of long silences before the voice agent replies. What helps most?
options: Use a larger LLM for better answers
Stream the reply and start speaking as the first sentence arrives
Add hold music
Ask callers to speak more slowly
multimodal.why: Waiting for the full reply before speaking adds seconds. Streaming into text-to-speech cuts perceived delay.

multimodal.q: You tested a voice agent with clean studio audio. Real users call from warehouses on speakerphone. What next?
options: Nothing, the tests passed
Only test with more studio audio
Ask users to find a quiet room
Test with realistic noisy recordings before launch
multimodal.why: Real conditions differ from the lab. Test with the audio your users actually produce.

multimodal.q: A team reuses its chat prompt for the voice agent. What problem usually appears?
options: Long, formatted answers with bullets that sound awful read aloud
The agent stops using tools
Speech-to-text stops working
Costs drop too much
multimodal.why: Voice needs short, spoken-style answers. Markdown lists and long paragraphs do not work when heard.

responsibleai.q: What is the NIST AI RMF?
options: A US framework to help organisations manage AI risks
A European law that bans all AI
A model training library
A certificate every AI engineer must hold
responsibleai.why: It is voluntary guidance for mapping, measuring and managing AI risk. The EU AI Act is the binding law.

responsibleai.q: What does meaningful human oversight require?
options: A person clicking approve on every output
No humans at all, for consistency
A reviewer with the time, context and authority to disagree
A monthly report nobody reads
responsibleai.why: Oversight only counts if the human can actually catch and override errors.

responsibleai.q: Crestview Lending wants an AI to pre-screen loan applications. When should fairness testing start?
options: After launch, if complaints arrive
At design time, testing outcomes across groups before launch
Only if a regulator asks
Never, models are neutral
responsibleai.why: Governance is design input. Testing early lets you change features or thresholds before harm happens.

responsibleai.q: Crestview's COO asks you: 'Is our tool high-risk under the EU AI Act?' How do you answer?
options: Give a firm legal yes or no yourself
Say the act does not apply to banks
Tell them to ignore it until enforcement
Explain the framework's categories and point them to their legal team for the final call
responsibleai.why: FDEs explain how the rules work but do not give legal conclusions. Compliance decisions belong to the customer's lawyers.

responsibleai.q: A reviewer approves 400 AI decisions an hour and has never rejected one. What is the problem?
options: The human in the loop is a rubber stamp, not real oversight
The reviewer is too slow
The model needs more features
Nothing, this shows the model is perfect
responsibleai.why: Oversight with no time or real disagreement gives false comfort. Reduce volume or sample and measure reviewer agreement.

case.q: In a case interview, what is the first move with a vague prompt like 'use AI to cut discharge delays'?
options: Pick a model and sketch the architecture
Restate the goal and ask what 'better' means
Estimate the GPU budget
List every AI technique you know
case.why: Restating and clarifying shows you listen and often reveals that the stated ask is really a guess at a solution.

options: The main metric the sponsor pays for
A metric that measures model speed only
A metric that must not get worse while you improve the main one
A metric used only in the demo
case.why: A guardrail stops you from winning on one number by breaking something else, such as readmission rate while cutting discharge time.

case.q: Mapleton Hospital says 'discharges take too long'. On day one, what should you do?
options: Start building a chatbot for nurses
Shadow a case manager on real discharges and file the data access request
Write a 30-page architecture document
Ask IT to buy a vector database
case.why: Watching real work reveals where delays hide, and data access is usually the slowest part, so start it in parallel right away.

case.q: A sponsor wants a full AI platform across all 12 wards. How do you scope the first release?
options: Build all 12 wards at once to show ambition
Refuse until the data is perfect
Build a demo on fake data for every ward
Propose a thin slice: one ward, one bottleneck, real data, end to end
case.why: A thin slice solves one real problem end to end in production conditions, which proves value fast and teaches you what to scale.

case.q: A candidate's case answer skips straight to a model choice and never states a baseline. What is the main problem?
options: Without a baseline there is no way to prove the work added value
Model choice should always come after pricing
Baselines are only needed for research papers
The answer was too short for the interviewer
case.why: A baseline is the value before any change. Without it you cannot show impact, and opening with the model skips the real problem.

options: A question that suggests the answer you want to hear
The first question in an interview guide
A question asked to the most senior person
A question about the budget
discovery.why: Leading questions like 'Wouldn't automation be faster?' push polite people to agree, so you learn little.

discovery.q: What is the end product of customer discovery?
options: A signed contract
A working prototype
A clear problem statement grounded in real evidence
A list of every feature users asked for
discovery.why: Discovery ends in a problem statement: who has the problem, what it is, how much it costs and why it matters now.

discovery.q: At Riverbend Utilities, a billing clerk says 'the system is slow'. How do you find the real cause?
options: Tell them your product will fix it
Ask why repeatedly until you reach a cause you can act on
Move on to the next interviewee
Ask whether they would like an AI assistant
discovery.why: The five whys digs past the first symptom. The first answer is rarely the root cause.

discovery.q: You have interviewed only the VP who funds the project at Cobalt Freight. What should you do next?
options: Write the problem statement now
Start building to save time
Send the VP a survey
Shadow the dispatchers who do the daily work
discovery.why: The sponsor knows the goal, but daily users know where the pain really is. Watching them reveals skipped steps and workarounds.

discovery.q: Which interview question is the classic discovery mistake?
options: 'Walk me through what you did last Tuesday.'
'How do you handle an order that fails?'
'Would you use a tool that did this automatically?'
'What happened the last time this broke?'
discovery.why: Hypothetical 'would you use...' questions get polite yes answers. Ask about what people actually did recently instead.

exec.q: What does 'answer first' mean in an executive update?
options: Start with the technical root cause analysis
Put the main conclusion in the first line, then the support
Answer every question they asked in order
Reply within one minute of any email
exec.why: Executives often read only the first lines, so the answer must lead. SCQA and the pyramid principle order the rest.

exec.q: Why translate 'recall went from 71% to 93%' for an executive?
options: Executives buy outcomes like risk, cost and throughput, not ML metrics
Recall is confidential
Executives prefer longer explanations
Percentages are not allowed in updates
exec.why: Converting a metric into its business effect, like far fewer wrong-policy answers, makes the value clear to the decision maker.

exec.q: The CIO of Sterling Mutual emails: 'Your assistant is completely broken.' What do you do first?
options: Reply with a detailed architecture explanation
Wait until you know the root cause before replying
Acknowledge, restate the business impact and commit to an update time
Forward it to your manager and stay quiet
exec.why: Listening and restating lowers the temperature. Then you triage, restore service and send a short answer-first update.

exec.q: During an outage, you can restore service with a workaround in two hours or ship a full fix in three days. What do you do?
options: Wait for the full fix so it is done properly
Ship the workaround now, then do the root-cause fix
Do neither until the CIO approves in writing
Roll back all features from the last year
exec.why: Restore service first. A workaround in hours beats a perfect fix in days, and the root-cause fix can follow.

exec.q: Which is the classic mistake when an angry executive calls?
options: Restating their business impact
Promising the next update time
Sending a short answer-first summary
Opening with a technical deep-dive and a guessed root cause
exec.why: A technical deep-dive confuses, and promising a root cause before you have one damages trust if it turns out wrong.

docs.q: What question does a statement of work (SOW) answer?
options: How will the engineers build it?
What are we paying for, by when and how will it be accepted?
Why did we choose this database?
Who attended the kickoff meeting?
docs.why: The SOW is a contract document: scope, deliverables, timeline, acceptance criteria and fees.

docs.q: What belongs in a PRD rather than a design doc?
options: The database schema
The retry and caching strategy
The problem, the users and how success is measured
The deployment pipeline
docs.why: A PRD describes the problem and desired outcome, not the code. The design doc covers how it will be built.

docs.q: A draft SOW for Alder Retail says the deliverable is 'an AI solution'. What should you add?
options: Specific deliverables and measurable acceptance criteria
A longer company history section
More marketing language about AI
A list of every tool you might use
docs.why: Vague deliverables invite scope creep and payment disputes. Acceptance criteria say exactly when the work counts as done.

docs.q: In a hallway chat, Alder's manager asks you to add a second region to the pilot and you agree. What should happen next?
options: Nothing, a verbal yes is enough
Quietly build it and hope timelines hold
Tell the engineers but not the sponsor
Log the decision and update the SOW or raise a change request
docs.why: Untracked scope changes cause disputes later. A decision log and SOW update keep everyone aligned on cost and timing.

docs.q: A teammate writes the design doc after the code is finished. What is the problem?
options: Design docs must be longer than the code
The doc never influenced the decision or caught risks early
Design docs are only for executives
Nothing, this is the recommended order
docs.why: A design doc exists to compare alternatives and catch problems before building. Written afterwards, it only describes.

demo.q: What is the 'before and after' structure in a demo?
options: Showing the old product version, then the new one
Showing today's painful task, then the same task with your system
Demoing to executives, then to users
Reading the agenda, then the summary
demo.why: Showing the pain first makes the improvement obvious. Keep the comparison fair: same task, same data.

demo.q: How should a demo for executives differ from one for end users?
options: Executives get more features and more screens
There should be no difference at all
Lead with the result and rollout; users want to see their exact workflow
Executives should see only the code
demo.why: Executives care about outcomes, cost, risk and timing. End users care whether it fits their daily work.

demo.q: Tomorrow you demo to Oakridge Clinic over unreliable hotel Wi-Fi. What should you prepare?
options: A screen recording and cached responses as a fallback for each live step
A longer introduction to fill time if it breaks
A new feature to impress them
Nothing, apologise if it fails
demo.why: Planning a fallback for each live step turns a failure into a thirty-second pause instead of a lost meeting.

demo.q: You have ten minutes with Oakridge's COO. Your product has 25 features. What do you show?
options: All 25 features quickly
The settings and admin screens
The architecture diagram only
One real user workflow told as a story, then the ask
demo.why: One workflow done well beats a feature tour. Leave time for the closing ask.

demo.q: Which is the classic demo mistake?
options: Using realistic data from discovery
Clicking through every screen with no user or story in mind
Rehearsing with a timer
Ending with a clear next step
demo.why: Feature tours lose the audience. A story about one real user shows why the product matters.

moat.q: In AI products, what is a data moat?
options: A firewall around the customer's database
Proprietary process data from real use that competitors cannot copy
A large public dataset anyone can download
An encrypted backup of the model
moat.why: Features can be copied from a demo. Records of how real work gets done, like corrections and decisions, cannot.

moat.q: What is the difference between COGS and R&D?
options: They are two names for the same cost
COGS is research; R&D is hosting
COGS is the cost of serving one customer; R&D improves the product for all
R&D is only spent on salaries
moat.why: Custom one-off work lands in COGS and hurts margins. Work that helps every customer is R&D and builds value.

moat.q: Fernway Logistics asks for a special approval rule no other customer needs. Where should it go?
options: Isolate it in configuration or an owned adapter
Fork the core product for Fernway
Hard-code it into the main codebase
Refuse because it is a one-off
moat.why: Config or an adapter with a named owner isolates the one-off so it cannot break anything else.

moat.q: Three customers now ask for the same export connector. What do you do?
options: Build three separate custom versions
Tell them to write it themselves
Keep it as a one-off for the first customer only
Bring product the evidence of repetition and a draft design for the core
moat.why: Repetition across customers is the signal to generalize. Bring evidence so it becomes a product feature.

moat.q: Which pattern is the trap the lesson warns about?
options: Using config for customer thresholds
Letting FDEs become the permanent support desk for a customer
Giving each adapter a named owner
Collecting user corrections as training data
moat.why: An escalation crutch ties up FDEs forever and stops the customer from owning the system.

change.q: What is a champion in an adoption plan?
options: The executive who signs the contract
A respected user who helps peers adopt the tool
The vendor's sales lead
The person who resists the change most
change.why: Champions are trusted colleagues who answer questions, share tips and bring feedback back to the team.

change.q: Which is a real adoption measure?
options: Number of licenses bought
Number of logins in week one
Share of real tasks done in the new tool
Number of training invites sent
change.why: Adoption means real work moves to the tool. Logins and licenses can grow while work stays in the old spreadsheet.

change.q: Senior adjusters at Fairlane Mutual refuse the new tool. What do you do first?
options: Ask what the tool breaks or slows for them
Escalate to their boss to force use
Remove the old system overnight
Ignore them and focus on new hires
change.why: Resistance is information. Their objections often reveal real gaps in the tool or workflow.

change.q: Go-live is in six weeks. When should most user training happen?
options: All in one big session today
Only after launch if people ask
Never, the tool is intuitive
Close to go-live, on users' real tasks, with follow-up help
change.why: Training too early is forgotten. Short, task-based sessions near launch, plus support, stick better.

change.q: A dashboard shows 90% of Fairlane users logged in, but claims are still handled in the old spreadsheet. The mistake?
options: Too few licenses
Counting logins as adoption instead of real work in the tool
The dashboard is too slow
Training started too late
change.why: Logins are not usage. Measure tasks completed in the new tool.

options: A list of Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Dependencies
A record of server failures
A backup of the code repository
A list of team holidays
pm.why: A RAID log tracks what could go wrong, what you assume, current problems and what you depend on, each with an owner.

pm.q: In MoSCoW prioritisation, what does 'Must' mean?
options: Nice to have if time allows
Agreed not to do this time
Without it the release fails or has no value
Important, but there is a workaround
pm.why: Must items are essential. Should, Could and Won't come after, so the real Musts do not slip.

pm.q: The Marlowe Retail project needs a firewall rule from their IT team to proceed. How do you handle it?
options: Wait quietly until IT acts
Track it as a dependency with an owner and a due date
Work around security controls
Blame IT in the final report
pm.why: Customer dependencies cause most FDE delays. Give them owners and dates like any other task and chase early.

pm.q: Week 6 of 10: data access is two weeks late and the deadline is now at risk. What status do you report?
options: Green, since you might catch up
Red only in the final week
No report until it is resolved
Amber now, with the cause, impact and what you need
pm.why: Reporting amber early builds trust and gives time to act. Jumping from green to red late destroys it.

pm.q: Which delivery habit is the trap?
options: Ending each sprint with a demo
Writing user stories with acceptance criteria
Marking every request as a Must
Sending a weekly status report
pm.why: If everything is a Must, nothing is. Prioritise honestly so the essentials ship.

options: The time until total benefits cover the total cost
The length of the contract
The time to build the system
The time until the first invoice
roi.why: Payback tells a CFO how long the money is at risk before the project pays for itself.

roi.q: What does a sensitivity analysis show?
options: Which users are most sensitive to change
How the result changes if key assumptions are wrong
The model's accuracy on sensitive data
How fast the system responds
roi.why: Testing lower adoption or smaller savings shows whether the case still holds when you are wrong.

roi.q: A tool saves Pembrook Claims staff 2,000 hours a year, but no one is let go or overtime cut. How do you present it?
options: As 2,000 hours of cash saved at full salary
As zero value
As capacity freed up for other work, a softer benefit
As a headcount reduction
roi.why: Saved hours are not saved cash unless spending drops. Call it capacity freed and say what it enables.

roi.q: You are building Pembrook's business case. Which cost is most often forgotten?
options: The first build sprint
The pilot team's kickoff meeting
The laptop used for coding
Running costs like LLM tokens, monitoring and maintainers
roi.why: The full cost of an AI system includes ongoing running and people costs, not just the build.

roi.q: A business case assumes all 500 agents use the tool fully from day one. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, it keeps the math simple
Adoption ramps up over time, so benefits are overstated
500 agents is too few for AI
ROI cannot be calculated with agents
roi.why: Real adoption grows gradually. Model a ramp and test lower adoption in the sensitivity analysis.

arc.q: What are the four phases of the course's 12-week engagement arc?
options: Sell, build, bill, renew
Design, code, test, deploy
Scope, prototype, harden, hand over
Discover, fundraise, hire, launch
arc.why: Scope (weeks 1-2), prototype (3-6), harden (7-10) and hand over (11-12), each with a clear output.

arc.q: What does SMART stand for in success criteria?
options: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Simple, Modern, Automated, Robust, Tested
Scalable, Managed, Accurate, Reliable, Trusted
Strategic, Minimal, Agile, Rapid, Technical
arc.why: A SMART criterion names the team, metric, baseline, target, deadline and where the number comes from.

arc.q: In week 1 at Glenmore Insurance, IT says data access will take a month. What do you do?
options: Build the whole pilot on fake data and swap later
File the access request on day one and scope with samples meanwhile
Delay the project start by a month
Copy data from a personal laptop
arc.why: Access is often the slowest part. Starting the request immediately keeps it from blocking the prototype.

arc.q: At the end of hardening, the team wants to change how 'handling time' is defined. What is the risk?
options: None, better definitions always help
It makes the dashboard load slower
It requires a new SOW
The comparison with the baseline becomes meaningless
arc.why: Measure the result exactly as you measured the baseline. Changing definitions midway breaks the comparison and trust.

arc.q: Which is the trap in a new engagement?
options: Naming a baseline metric in discovery
Training a client Center of Excellence
Proposing 'let's build a RAG bot' before any baseline exists
Choosing one pilot team and workflow
arc.why: Jumping to a solution before you know the pain and the baseline means you cannot prove value later.

pod.q: In the course's pod model, what does the Echo do?
options: Writes most of the production code
Owns the customer relationship, scoping and admin
Runs the model training cluster
Reviews every architecture decision centrally
pod.why: The Echo is the Deployment Strategist. The two Deltas are the engineers who write the code.

options: Days from contract signature to the first measurable customer value
Time for a model to finish training
Hours an engineer spends per ticket
Time between two releases
pod.why: TTV is the pod's headline metric because it captures both speed and real impact.

pod.q: Your pod's engineers at Quarry Foods spend half their week on status calls and access tickets. What fixes this?
options: Hire a third engineer to write reports
Cancel all customer meetings
The Echo absorbs admin so the Deltas stay on engineering
Ask engineers to work weekends
pod.why: Protecting engineers from admin drag is a core Echo job. Unprotected, it can eat 40 to 60% of their time.

pod.q: Leadership tells your pod: 'cut invoice exceptions by 30% this quarter, because renewal depends on it.' How should the pod work?
options: Wait for a detailed plan from headquarters
Submit each decision to a central review board
Build every feature on the original roadmap
Choose its own approach to hit that intent
pod.why: Mission-type tactics: leaders give the objective and the reason, and the team on site picks the method.

options: Shipping small features and keeping those users adopt
Tracking TTV and adoption
Measuring the pod by features shipped instead of value delivered
Giving the pod a clear outcome and reason
pod.why: Counting features rewards output, not impact. Value delivered and adoption are the measures that matter.

options: Sending the contract to the customer
Getting a working product to run in one customer's messy environment
Training the sales team
Writing marketing copy for launch
lastmile.why: The name comes from delivery: the final stretch to the door is the hardest. Undocumented APIs, broken schemas and exceptions stall it.

lastmile.q: What is a typed wrapper around an API?
options: A small module that hides the API's quirks behind a clean, checked interface
A PDF describing the API
A firewall rule for API traffic
A new version of the customer's API
lastmile.why: Only the wrapper knows about the messy API. The product gets predictable, validated objects.

lastmile.q: Hollis Manufacturing's ERP API has no documentation. What do you do first?
options: Guess the fields and ship to production
Ask for a sandbox, probe carefully and save real responses as test fixtures
Wait until their vendor writes documentation
Rewrite their ERP system
lastmile.why: Learn by observation, save every response, and build a wrapper with tests against those fixtures.

lastmile.q: At Hollis, 'orders over 50,000 go to Priya for approval' is an unwritten rule. How should you encode it?
options: Fork the product code for Hollis
Ignore it until users complain
Ask Priya to approve everything
As a configurable rule outside the core code
lastmile.why: Exceptions belong in rules or config the customer can see and change, not in a product fork.

lastmile.q: Your team rebuilds the same CRM connector from scratch for each new customer. What is the fix?
options: Assign a new engineer each time
Keep doing it; every customer is unique
Turn it into a reusable playbook template and push common parts into the product
Stop supporting that CRM
lastmile.why: A fix used once is wasted. Playbooks and templates make the tenth onboarding faster than the first.

options: Knowing many prompt tricks
Holding several AI certificates
Using AI tools well on real work, with judgement and verification
Being able to train a model from scratch
fluency.why: Fluency is behaviour: knowing when to use AI, how to direct it and how to check what it produces.

fluency.q: Where should an FDE learning route start?
options: From the requirements in real FDE job posts
From the longest course catalogue
From whatever is trending this week
From the most advanced math course
fluency.why: Start from the job: list recurring skills from job posts and mark each as strong, partial or missing.

fluency.q: You need to draft a customer-facing summary at work. Using the 4Ds, what comes first?
options: Paste everything into the tool and send the result
Delegation: decide which parts AI does well and which you must own
Ask a friend to review it
Write it all by hand to be safe
fluency.why: Delegation comes first. Then you describe the task well, check the output with discernment and stay diligent about responsibility.

fluency.q: A colleague wants to paste Veridian Health patient notes into a free chatbot to summarise them. What do you say?
options: Fine, as long as the summary is accurate
Only paste half the notes
Remove the dates first and then paste
Stop: use only tools your employer has approved for that data
fluency.why: Customer and patient data must stay in approved tools. Accuracy does not fix a data-handling violation.

fluency.q: Which is the common learning-path trap?
options: Building a project to show each skill
Applying new skills to one work task a week
Collecting certificates with no project or work sample to show
Picking courses based on job posts
fluency.why: Certificates alone prove little. Hiring managers want to see working projects and results.

interview.q: Which pillar carries the most weight in the course's FDE interview blueprint?
options: Business acumen
Customer scenario and communication
Algorithm puzzles
Deep technical understanding
interview.why: Deep technical is 40%, practical implementation 30%, customer scenario 20% and business acumen 10%.

interview.q: What does NRR (net revenue retention) measure?
options: Revenue kept and grown from existing customers over a year
New customers signed per quarter
Profit per engineer
Time from contract to value
interview.why: NRR includes expansion and losses from current customers. FDE work that drives adoption pushes it up.

interview.q: In a scenario round, the 'customer' says: 'We want AI to improve our supply chain.' What do you do first?
options: Propose an LLM agent architecture
Quote a price
Ask discovery questions to find the specific pain and metric
Explain how transformers work
interview.why: The round scores discovery and scoping. Jumping to a solution is the most common failure.

interview.q: An interviewer keeps asking 'why' about your vector search until you are unsure. How should you answer?
options: Invent a confident answer
Explain what you know in layers and say clearly where your knowledge ends
Change the subject to your strongest project
Say the question is unfair
interview.why: Follow-ups probe your edge. A layered answer and honest limits score better than a made-up detail.

interview.q: Which is a classic FDE interview prep mistake?
options: Mapping STAR stories to the four pillars
Practising a timed build
Preparing numbers from portfolio evals
Spending most prep time on algorithm puzzles
interview.why: DSA is a small part of an FDE loop. Keep it warm, but spend most time in proportion to the pillar weights.

dsa.q: What is the average time to check if a key is in a Python dict?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n squared)
dsa.why: Dicts and sets use hashing, so lookups are constant time on average. Checking 'x in list' is O(n).

dsa.q: Which data structure is first in, first out?
options: Stack
Heap
Queue
Hash map
dsa.why: A queue serves items in arrival order. A stack is last in, first out.

dsa.q: You must find the 10 slowest API calls out of 5 million log lines. Which approach fits best?
options: Sort all 5 million lines, then take the top 10
Keep a heap of size 10 while scanning once
Compare every pair of lines
Use binary search on the unsorted log
dsa.why: A size-k heap gives top-k in O(n log k) with little memory, better than sorting everything.

dsa.q: You need the fewest hops between two services in a dependency graph. Which algorithm?
options: Depth-first search
Binary search
Bubble sort
Breadth-first search
dsa.why: BFS explores level by level, so the first time it reaches the target is via the fewest edges in an unweighted graph.

dsa.q: A candidate's loop calls list.pop(0) on every step. What is the hidden problem?
options: pop(0) is not valid Python
pop(0) is O(n), so the loop quietly becomes O(n squared)
It removes the last item instead
Lists cannot be used in loops
dsa.why: Removing from the front shifts every item. Use collections.deque with popleft() for O(1).

builddrill.q: In a 90-minute build drill, what is the biggest block of time for?
options: Choosing a framework
Writing the README
The core end-to-end path
Adding authentication
builddrill.why: The suggested plan gives about 30 minutes to the core path. Setup should be fast because you practised it.

builddrill.q: Which things should you usually cut or stub in a build drill?
options: Authentication, databases and polish
Input validation and error handling
Tests and the README
The one working end-to-end path
builddrill.why: Keep one working path, validation, basic errors, a couple of tests and a README. Stub the rest and say so.

builddrill.q: Ten minutes into a live build for a claims API, you are unsure if inputs can be missing. What do you do?
options: Guess and move on silently
Ask a quick clarifying question that changes what you build
Stop and write a long spec
Build both versions just in case
builddrill.why: A few targeted clarifying questions show FDE instincts. Too many eat your time.

builddrill.q: You have 10 minutes left and skipped retries and a database. How do you present this?
options: Hide the shortcuts and hope nobody asks
Apologise for not finishing everything
Rush to add a database in the last minutes
Show it working, run the tests, and explain each trade-off and next step
builddrill.why: Named trade-offs turn shortcuts into evidence of judgement: what you did, why, the risk and what comes next.

builddrill.q: Which is the classic build-drill trap?
options: Running the code early and often
Spending 40 minutes on setup and a fancy architecture
Writing two quick tests
Talking through your reasoning
builddrill.why: Burning time on setup leaves nothing for the core path. Practise scaffolding until it takes under ten minutes.

casebank.q: In the case practice rubric, what does a strong 'first slice' look like?
options: A full platform covering every department
Shippable in weeks, narrow, with a human in the loop
A slide deck with no build
A research study lasting a year
casebank.why: A narrow slice with human review proves value fast and keeps risk low.

casebank.q: Roughly how many clarifying questions does the bank suggest before committing to a plan?
options: None; start with the solution
About fifteen, to be thorough
Three to five sharp ones that change the plan
One, then assume the rest
casebank.why: A few targeted questions show structure. Too many and you never commit to a plan.

casebank.q: Case: a vendor's AI assistant at Greyhaven Energy's call centre has 15% usage. Your first two weeks?
options: Rebuild it with a newer model immediately
Add five new features to attract users
Recommend cancelling the contract
Learn what success meant, study usage by team and talk to agents who stopped
casebank.why: A rescue is about diagnosis and adoption first. Users who quit tell you the real blockers.

casebank.q: Mid-case, the interviewer challenges your assumption that labelled data exists. What is the best reaction?
options: Thank them, adjust the plan and say what changes
Defend the assumption for several minutes
Ignore it and keep presenting
Say the case cannot be solved
casebank.why: Adapting to pushback is a strong signal. Defending a weak assumption at length is worse than changing course.

casebank.q: A candidate opens a permit-processing case by choosing an LLM and a vector database. What is the mistake?
options: The LLM choice was too small
They should have picked a graph database
Jumping to architecture before knowing the user, workflow or metric
Nothing, speed is scored highly
casebank.why: Solutions before questions is the most costly mistake across cases.

sqlbank.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: They are identical
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups
WHERE works only on text columns
sqlbank.why: Use HAVING for conditions on aggregates like COUNT(*) > 5, since WHERE runs before grouping.

sqlbank.q: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: All rows from the left table, with matches from the right or NULLs
Only rows that match in both tables
All rows from both tables
Only rows with no match
sqlbank.why: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL.

sqlbank.q: Ridgeway Retail wants each customer's most recent order. Which approach fits best?
options: SELECT DISTINCT on customer_id
GROUP BY order_id
ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by customer, ordered by date desc; keep row 1
A CROSS JOIN of customers and orders
sqlbank.why: A window function ranks orders within each customer, so you can keep the latest one with all its columns.

sqlbank.q: A revenue report doubled after you joined orders to a shipments table. What most likely happened?
options: The database cached old results
SUM is broken for large tables
The WHERE clause was missing a semicolon
Orders with several shipments were repeated by the join, inflating the sum
sqlbank.why: A one-to-many join multiplies rows. Aggregate shipments first, or join at the right grain.

sqlbank.q: A query uses WHERE discount = NULL and returns no rows, though many discounts are missing. What is wrong?
options: Comparing with = NULL is never true; use IS NULL
NULL values cannot be stored in numeric columns
The column must be renamed
WHERE cannot be used with numbers
sqlbank.why: NULL means unknown, so = NULL is not true for any row. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

career.q: What makes a resume bullet an 'impact bullet'?
options: It lists your job duties clearly
It names every tool you used
It is under five words long
Action verb, what you built, and a measurable result
career.why: Duties say what your job was. Impact bullets say what changed because of you.

options: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Skill, Tool, Approach, Review
Summary, Timeline, Achievement, Reference
Strategy, Tactic, Assessment, Response
career.why: Most of a STAR answer's time should go on Action, and the Result ideally has a number.

career.q: You search job boards only for 'Forward Deployed Engineer' and find few roles. What should you do?
options: Wait for more FDE postings
Apply to unrelated roles
Also search Solutions Engineer, AI Engineer and Deployment Strategist
Only apply through cold emails
career.why: The same work appears under several titles. Read the description for customer-facing and deployment work.

career.q: A recruiter at Lumora Analytics asks your salary expectation in the first call. A good response?
options: Give a low number to seem easy to hire
Say you want to understand the role and level first and ask the budgeted range
Refuse to continue the call
Give your current salary plus 5%
career.why: Negotiation starts with a written offer. Early on, learn the role and range before naming numbers.

career.q: Which resume bullet shows the trap the lesson warns about?
options: 'Cut report time 60% by building a dbt pipeline'
'Shipped a RAG pilot used by 40 agents'
'Reduced API errors from 5% to 0.5%'
'Responsible for data pipelines'
career.why: It lists a duty, not a result. Also never inflate numbers you cannot explain in an interview.

options: Trains a new model on every question
Searches documents for relevant passages, then has the model answer using them
Generates random answers and ranks them
Compresses documents into one summary
projecta.why: Retrieval grounds the answer in real passages, which reduces made-up answers.

options: It uses a GPU
It has a web interface
It checks its evidence and can rewrite a weak query and retry
It answers in several languages
projecta.why: A grader decides whether passages suffice. If not, the graph rewrites the query and searches again.

projecta.q: A user at Dunmore Legal sees passages from a document they are not allowed to read. What was missed?
options: Filtering retrieval by the ACL stored with each chunk
Using a bigger generation model
Raising the similarity threshold
Adding more chunks per query
projecta.why: Each chunk stores the groups allowed to see it. Retrieval must filter by the user's groups before generation.

projecta.q: You demo Project A to a hiring manager. What makes it most convincing?
options: A long list of libraries used
Screenshots of the code
A live chat with no measurements
Numbers: faithfulness, p95 latency and cost per 1,000 queries
projecta.why: Evaluations turn a demo into evidence. Have baseline vs. improved numbers ready.

projecta.q: Your agent keeps rewriting and retrying a query forever on hard questions. What is the missing safeguard?
options: A larger embedding model
A retry cap on the rewrite loop
More documents in the index
A faster database
projecta.why: Without a cap, loops can run forever and burn cost. Cap retries and then answer with what you have or say you do not know.

projectb.q: Why does the Project B agent use search and read tools instead of pasting the repo into the prompt?
options: Repos are too large, and pasting wastes tokens and buries useful lines
Tools make the agent slower on purpose
LLMs cannot read code
Pasting code is against licensing rules
projectb.why: grep_files then open_file brings in only the relevant lines, saving tokens and improving focus.

projectb.q: In LangGraph, what is a node?
options: A GPU server
A saved prompt template
A Python function that reads state and returns the fields it changed
A test file in the repo
projectb.why: Nodes are steps, edges are allowed moves, and LangGraph merges each node's update into the shared state.

projectb.q: After each task, your agent should learn a lesson for next time. Which ACE role writes down what went well or wrong?
options: Generator
Reflector
Retriever
Router
projectb.why: The Generator solves the task, the Reflector analyses the attempt, and the Curator updates the playbook.

projectb.q: After several rounds the playbook keeps getting shorter and loses specific tips. What is happening and what helps?
options: The model is too small; switch models
Tests are failing; skip them
Nothing, shorter is always better
Context collapse; apply small incremental updates instead of full rewrites
projectb.why: Rewriting the whole context each round compresses it and drops hard-won detail. Add or edit individual bullets instead.

projectb.q: Which is a Project B design trap?
options: Logging tokens per task
Recording pass rate per round
Letting the Generator and test loop retry with no cap
Using focused prompts per role
projectb.why: An uncapped fix-and-test loop can run forever and burn tokens. Set a retry limit.
